article.markdown:
# A site photo log exposed two gaps in my photo components

> **Build log series**: I hand my own design system `@gunjo/ui` ([Gunjo](https://gunjo.jp)) to an AI that has never seen it, and have it build real screens. This is the second construction screen. The brief: a **construction photo log screen for a site supervisor**. The screen covers photos organized by date, type of work, and location, along with filters, a lightbox, before-and-after correction photos from inspections, and photo selection for reports.

## Result: 4/5. Photo components covered most of a construction log

The agent started with only the public npm package and the gunjo.jp docs. The finished photo log passes `tsc` and adapts to both mobile and desktop layouts.

**Components added to Gunjo for photo management (digital asset management) needed almost no adaptation for a construction photo log**. They were intended for managing an asset library, but they became the core of a photo log in a different industry.

- **`AssetGrid` (photo grid)**: it lays out thumbnails, supports multi-select, and exposes `renderMeta`, a render prop for badges showing the type or stage of work beneath each photo. It fit the log grid particularly well.
- **`AssetInspectorPanel` (detail panel)**: it accepts arbitrary fields, comments, and classification tags, so the desktop side panel could display the construction photo board details (project name, type of work, survey point, and date taken) directly.
- **`MediaPickerDialog` (multi-select dialog)**: it supported the report workflow of "build a log from the selected photos" as-is.
- **`FileUploader` (upload)**: it already covers accepted file types, file count, size, and progress, so it handled photo intake outright.

The existing catalog covered the photo grid, filtering, upload, and report selection on its own.

## What was missing: construction details in the lightbox and before-and-after photos

Two areas remained uncovered, and both have a clear scope.

1. **The lightbox cannot show the construction photo board details.** `MediaLightbox` is already polished, with zoom, previous and next navigation, and support for portrait images, but **the information shown beside it is fixed to file attributes (dimensions, type, size, creation date, and rating)**. A construction photo needs work information such as the type of work, survey point, location, and comments, but there is no way to pass that in. This time I hand-rolled a custom lightbox. The image viewer itself works well, so this gap would close if it could accept work-specific details.
2. **There is no component for showing correction photos as a pair.** I wanted to place the before and after photos side by side for an issue found during an inspection, but there is no component for that. Similar components exist, but none are meant for comparing the same subject before and after a correction. I hand-rolled this part too.

The hand-rolled portion was about 140 lines out of roughly 900 for the whole screen, so it remained a minority of the implementation. I built most of the screen by composing existing components. I follow the rule of three: a missing component gets built for real only after three separate screens have needed it independently. These two are still at one.

## Where the names and entry points got confusing

- **The name `Gallery` is confusing.** It sounds like a grid of photos, but the component is actually a single-item viewer with one large image and a strip of thumbnails. `AssetGrid` is the grid for a photo log. I almost chose `Gallery` first and took a detour.
- **The by-use-case table has no entry for photo, image, or media management.** The photo management components at the center of this screen could not be reached through the by-use-case table, a static table that maps what you want to build to the components for it. I found them only after reading the type definitions. Someone who starts from the use case of building a photo screen cannot reach the main components. That guidance needs improvement.

## Wrapping up

I built the foundation of this second construction screen from components designed for another purpose. My photo management components became the core of a construction photo log in a different industry. I found only two gaps: work-specific details in the lightbox and a comparison of photos before and after a correction. Once again, the general-purpose catalog covered most of the screen, while the missing pieces clustered around industry-specific needs.
